Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Rajan never expected a hospital room to undo him. For twenty-three years he had walked toward things that other men ran from—unexploded ordnance buried in rubble, pressure plates wired to school gates, the silent mathematics of a wire cut in the right sequence. He had been called unflappable, steady-handed, a man built for the worst moments. None of that mattered when he walked into his daughter Priya’s hospital room and the antiseptic smell hit him first, then the drip stand beside her bed, the needle taped to the back of her small brown hand. She was seven then, and the diagnosis was Burkitt lymphoma. The oncologist said the words and Rajan heard them as a timer counting down. He stood in the doorway and understood, for the first time in his adult life, that he could not fix this. He could not cut the right wire. He could not make his hands steady. He could only stand there while the smell of disinfectant filled his lungs and the drip clicked and the needle stayed in his daughter’s vein.

The treatment took nine months. Priya survived. Rajan did not.

In the years since, the memory of that room does not arrive like a story he tells himself. It arrives without warning, fully formed, across every sense at once. He will be standing in his own kitchen and suddenly the smell is there—that sharp, chemical hospital smell—and he is back, seeing the drip, the needle, the pale yellow of the wall, hearing the rhythmic click of the IV pump. The memory is not a recollection. It is a trap door. One moment he is making tea; the next he is in that room again, his chest tight, his palms wet, his heart slamming against his ribs as if it means to break through. He has learned that the triggers are everywhere. A child’s laugh in a grocery store can do it. The sight of a bandage. The clean, sterile scent of a public restroom that has been mopped with bleach. He has come to believe that his body is no longer his to control—that anything in his surroundings can reach inside him and pull that memory up from wherever it hides.

He has not told his wife this. He has not told anyone. What would he say? That he, a bomb disposal technician, a man whose job requires the kind of nerve most people cannot imagine, is undone by the smell of hand sanitizer? That he has to leave the room when his own grandchildren visit because the sound of a child playing makes his throat close? He has become certain that his reactions mean something terrible about him. He is weak. He is falling apart. The thing that happened to Priya was bad, but the way he has responded to it—the panic, the avoidance, the sleepless nights—feels like proof that he is not the man he thought he was. He used to believe he could handle anything. Now he believes he cannot stop bad things from happening, and that belief has settled into him like a toxin.

Sleep has become its own kind of vigilance. He lies awake night after night, not because he is thinking, but because he is listening. He tells himself he needs to stay alert, that something might happen, that he must be ready. He does not know what he is ready for. He only knows that closing his eyes feels like surrender. When he does finally drift off, he wakes gasping from dreams that are not dreams but replays—the hospital room, the needle, the click of the pump—and his body is already in fight-or-flight before his mind catches up.

At work, he is still competent. His hands do not shake when he kneels beside a device. His breathing stays even. But the moment he steps away from the scene, the moment the adrenaline drops, the hospital smell seems to follow him. He has started avoiding certain areas of the base. The medical wing. The parking lot near the pediatric clinic. He takes longer routes. He makes excuses. He has become a man who navigates his own life by avoiding its hidden triggers, and the cost is that his world has shrunk to a series of safe corridors he can walk without being ambushed by his own memory.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in his own living room. His daughter Priya, now twenty-two and healthy, brought her newborn son to visit. Rajan held the baby for thirty seconds before the smell of baby powder—clean, white, medical—sent him into a full sensory reliving. He handed the child back and walked out of the house without a word. He stood in the driveway, shaking, and understood that he could not keep living this way. He is afraid of what he might become if he does not change. He is afraid that his weakness will cost him the people he loves. But underneath that, what he really wants—what he cannot bring himself to say aloud—is to sleep through one night without the hospital room waiting for him in the dark.
